notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to your Return to Running training program

To get the most from this plan, please read all of the content each week.

The program starts with what should be a fairly safe and conservative volume of running. This initial volume is actually the hardest part of the whole program to judge because each injury is so different. You need to be able to walk around and complete your normal daily tasks, including walking up and down stairs with no pain, or almost no pain, before starting this program. A pain you would judge as 1/10 or 2/10 is ok. A pain which is causing you to limp will be exacerbated by even a small volume of running.

If you feel like you are ready to start running, but the first level in this plan (Run 1-minute / walk 1-minute x 5 reps) causes your symptoms to flare up, then you are not ready to start running yet. You should wait until your day-to-day pain is 2/10 or less before starting, and in the meantime work on the stretching, strengthening and rolling exercises in this plan.

Throughout this training plan you need to “Listen to your Body” If your injury flares up at all then you need to rest for extra days until it settles down to a 2/10 or less.

If you find that your injury flares up when you shift “up a level” in the plan, from 5 reps to 7 reps for example, then you should go back to the previous level which did not cause your injury to flare up and repeat that a further two times before trying to increase the level again.

Strength and stability – What exercises should you be doing this week?

Strength and Stability are two different things. Strength describes the ability to use your big “movement” muscles efficiently. Stability describes the fine-tuning and coordination of all the little muscles in your body to help keep you balanced.

The ability to stand on one foot with your eyes closed for 60 seconds requires you to have good stability – We are going to test this in a minute.

We will work on both strength and stability during this program. If you have a stable “core” when you run you are much less likely for your injury to recur.

Test your stability now

To get an understanding of stability, I want you to do this simple one minute test. Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- Less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

Write down your score for both legs. We will revisit this later in the program and see how you have improved.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Running Technique

One of the most important aspects of making a successful return to running is knowing that your running technique is efficient. Running with the correct technique reduces the stress and strain on your muscles and joints. This is a perfect time and opportunity to change your technique.

Making changes to your technique when you are running 50km or 100km a week can cause new issues to arise, as the changes, although ultimately beneficial, will be placing more stress on some parts of your body and less on others. This program starts with a very low volume of running and gradually increases, so it will allow your body time to adapt, and benefit from, any changes in your technique.

This video describes the basics of running technique.

The main things you should focus on when running are:

- Stand up tall

- Take short steps

- These two queues alone can make all the difference to your body.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week two

I hope your first week on the training plan went well, and you have already started to focus on your running technique.

Remember:

You need to be able to walk around and complete your normal daily tasks, including walking up and down stairs with no pain, or almost no pain.

Before you continue to week 2 assess your current level of pain.

If your pain level is 1/10 or 2/10 then you can continue on to the next week. Please be honest with yourself. A pain which is causing you to limp will be exacerbated by even a small volume of running. If this sounds like you. then stop running.

If the first week of the plan (Run 1-minute / walk 1-minute x 5 reps) caused your symptoms to flare up, then you need to stop running again. Continue with the stretching, strengthening and rolling exercises and wait until your day-to-day pain is 2/10 or less before starting back on week 1 again.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Did you watch last week’s running technique video?

The sooner you improve your running technique the better. It is a VITAL component in the quest to staying injury-free. If you missed it last week make sure you watch this video to learn how to run with good technique.

In the video I refer to the importance of “cadence”. Cadence is the number of steps per minute you take when you are running. If you want to learn more about cadence and how to measure and improve yours, read THIS ARTICLE

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week three

I hope that week 2 went well and that you are starting to see some light at the end of the tunnel.

Please note: You don’t have to do all of the strength and stability exercises back-to-back. You can spread them out throughout the day to suit your work/family/training diary. Do what works best for you, but make sure you do them all.

Consistency is the key.

notes.label: Technique
notes.text:
Don’t forget about your running technique. Stand up tall and take short steps.

If you missed it last week, you should also now be starting to work on your cadence as part of improving your technique. To learn more about cadence and how to measure and improve yours, read THIS ARTICLE

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week four

How are you feeling?

Have you been good with the stretching and rolling and manage to keep the niggles at bay?

There will be highs and lows during these first weeks of returning to run. Be persistent. Very few running injuries get better from prolonged rest. You need to take this proactive approach of a gradual return to running with walk/run intervals combined with regular body maintenance exercises to sort out y0ur body and become injury-free.

We have focused on running technique for the last three weeks. Make sure you keep it “front of mind” during every run.

Keep this little mantra running through your head – “stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall, short steps, stand up tall . . . “

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week five

Congratulations. You have made it to the half way point. You are well on your way to making a full return to running.

Stick with the program. Don’t get over-excited and try and skip a level or two. These gradual increments work, so stick with them.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week six

We are building up to 6-minute running intervals, and 36 minutes running volume this week so it will be starting to feel like you are actually running again. You should also be starting to feel like some of your running fitness is returning and hopefully also getting some of the endorphins and feel-good factor that running gives you.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week seven

You are nearly there! Keep up the good work. Don’t get impatient. Keeping chipping away with the gradual progressions.

I hope you have been good with the body maintenance and you have got all of those tight muscles under control, and you are starting to develop a stronger and more stable core.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week eight

This week we build up to 12 minute running intervals and 48 minutes of total running volume in a day. Only 3 more weeks and you will be back to “normal” running again.

I hope by now you are recognising the benefits of the body maintenance sessions, and that you realise these are important for all runners, not just injured runners.

Your running progress is easy to measure, you have built from 1-minute intervals up to 12-minute intervals over the first 8 weeks of this program. The progress of your body maintenance may not be as obvious. That is why we are going to retest your stability this week and compare it to your results from week 1.

Restest your stability now

Have you got your results written down from your stability test in week 1 of the program?

We are going to do the test again to see if you have improved

Stand on one leg, close your eyes. Start counting in seconds 1, 2, 3…………

How long did you last until you had to put your foot down?.

If you made it to

- less than 10… You have a lot of work to do

- 10 – 30 ……. Still not good. Your lack of hip stability might cause some injuries

- 30 – 45 …….. Better, but still room for improvement

- 60 seconds …….. Great. Keep doing what you are doing

How did you go? If you’ve been good with all of the Body Maintenance sessions, then your stability should have improved a lot during theese 8 weeks. This extra stability will help a huge amount in your ability to remain injury-free.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week nine

This week we have our first non-stop runs.

Nice work, your patience and persistence are paying off. It must be a great feeling to have made it this far. Those 1-minute intervals are becoming a distant memory.

If the results of your stability test last week weren’t as good as you wanted or expected, then you need to work even harder on your body maintenance sessions. Some people have a good natural level of stability, others don’t. If you are someone that finds the balancing exercises difficult, then you stand to benefit the most from them, so keep chipping away. More stability = less injuries.

notes.label: Info
notes.text:
Welcome to week ten – the final week!

Congratulations to everyone who has made it to the end of the training program. This means you are well on the way to getting rid of your injury forever.

The program finishes with alternating non-stop runs and interval runs. You will notice that the total running volume on the interval days is more than the running volume on the non-stop days. This is deliberate. Even though you have gradually built up your volume over the last 10 weeks, you are not completely out of the woods just yet.

You should continue to gradually build your volume and listen to your body. If you have a new niggle, then give it the attention it deserves. Running through niggles is probably what caused your injury in the first place, so don’t do that to yourself again.

I would highly recommend that you continue with aerobic running for another 8 weeks in order to build a proper base from which you can then increase your speed.

Don’t enter any races or events for at least another 8 weeks. Build your base, get stronger and fitter, so that when you do race, you can race properly with confidence and great results.

Where should your running go to from here?

If you have enjoyed this program (and you are currently not a member) we have a comprehensive range of trail and road training plans that you can now follow to continue your running journey. Our 10km road plan or 10km trail plan would be the perfect place to start.

Good luck and happy training.

Mark Green.

glossary.definition: The plan has been written with a day gap between each running session. This additional “recovery” time between runs is vital to reduce the risk of flare ups. You can change the days of the runs each week to suit your personal circumstances, but make sure you schedule the day gap between each run.
If you have a particularly busy or stressful week and haven’t been able to complete one of the runs, don’t try to play catch up. Continue where you left off when you have time.

All of the running in this program is done at an aerobic pace. Aerobic means “running with oxygen”, which means running at a pace where you can comfortably carry out a conversation in full sentences. Don’t run so slowly that it feels unnatural and therefore effects your technique, but don’t run too quickly either. Run at a comfortable natural pace that allows you to breathe easily.

These are short sessions of exercises including stretching, stability, strengthening and foam rolling which will make the biggest difference to your ability to remove the cause of your injury and allow you to stay injury-free. When you return to running, depending on the length of your break, you are probably going to develop some tight and stiff muscles. You are asking them to do more work than they have done for a while. By performing the regular Body Maintenance sessions each week you will help to relieve the tight muscles, and also start to improve your “core” stability.
